dialog.body: Public Works, this is Denise. Happy New Year, how can I help you?
Hi, yes, happy New Year. Um, my name is Leila Singh, I am a property manager, and I am calling because the water, it is just sitting in the lane again and nobody is doing nothing.
Okay, I'm sorry about that. Which lane are we talking about, and where's the water coming from?

It is not coming from nothing, that is the thing. No rain, no storm, it is dry this whole week. But there is a snowbank, a big one, from when the plow came, and it is sitting right on top of the catch basin. The drain. So the melting water cannot go down and it makes a big pool across the whole lane.
Got it. So the snowbank is covering the catch basin and the melt is pooling instead of draining.

Yes, exactly, exactly. And then at night it freezes, and in the morning is ice. The tenants are slipping, one lady almost fell with the groceries. I already told the owner and he says call the city, so I am calling the city.
Sure. And what's the address, or the nearest cross street?

Ay, you know, I prefer not to say the address on the cell phone, I am in the car with the speaker. Can I just describe? It is the lane behind the building, with the blue dumpsters, and the drain is at the low part of the lane.
Hmm, I do need a location to send a crew to. Is there a street the lane runs off of, or a landmark close by?

Okay, okay. I will send the photos, and I put the location in the message. I took many pictures, like six, you can see the snowbank, the drain under it, and the water all across. I can send them to you right now.

That works. I'll give you the Public Works email in a second, but first let me make sure I've got this right. Dry weather, no storm, catch basin buried under a plowed snowbank, water pooling across the lane and freezing overnight.
Yes, that is it. Exactly. And is not the first time this winter I see the water there, but this time is the worst, because of the snow.
Okay. Are you able to hear me alright? You're a little choppy.
[line breaks up] ...sorry, I am driving through the hill. Can you hear me now?
Yes, I've got you again. So what are you hoping for today?
I want to know, will you open a work order? Like a real one, with a number. And for what date? Because I cannot say to the tenants, oh, maybe somebody comes. I need a day.

Understood. Yes, I can open a work order for a blocked catch basin. Once it's in, it goes to the crew supervisor, and they schedule it. After the holiday they're working through a pile of snow-related requests, so I'd say it's likely early next week, but I can't promise a particular day from my desk.
Early next week. Okay. But can you put on the order that is ice, that is dangerous? So it is first?
I'll note the ice and the slipping hazard right on the request, that does help them prioritize. Now I do need the street for it. Even just the street name the lane connects to.
[pause] Okay. You are right. Let me think how to say it. The lane is off Admiral Kalbfus, near the corner, and the building is the three-story with the green door.
Okay, off Admiral Kalbfus Road, near the corner, three-story building with the green door. Is there a street number you can give me, or is it easier if I take it from the email?
I put the number in the email, with the pictures. Is better, I do not want to say it wrong in the car.
That's fine. Do you want me to call you back at a number once the order is entered, so you can confirm the date?
Yes, please. It is four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-nine.
Four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-eight-nine. Got it. And that's under Leila Singh, S-I-N-G-H?
Yes, Leila, L-E-I-L-A. Singh. Right.
Wait, wait, one second. [crosstalk] No, mija, I am on the phone. Sorry, Denise, my daughter is in the back seat and she is asking me something.
No problem, take your time.
She says, what does the lady on the phone look like? She is five, she thinks everybody on the phone has a face she has to know.
Well, tell her I have short brown hair and glasses, and a big mug of coffee on my desk right now.
She says okay, she likes the coffee. Anyway. Sorry. So the email, what is it?

Easiest thing is to go to the city website, the Public Works page, and the contact email is listed right there at the top. Put in the subject line, catch basin blocked, with the street name, and attach all six pictures.
Okay, I will do it when I park. And you will see them today?
I'll enter the request now with what you've told me, and when your photos come in I'll attach them to it. That way the crew sees the snowbank and the ice before they head out.
Okay. Good. Because honestly, I call and call about this kind of thing, and they say yes yes, and then nothing. I am a little tired of it.
I hear you. This one will have a number on it, and I'll call you back at that cell with the scheduled date. If you haven't heard from me by Tuesday, call this line and ask for me.
Tuesday. Okay. Denise, right? D-E-N...
Denise, yes. D-E-N-I-S-E.
Okay. Thank you. And in the meantime I will put salt on the ice, but the water, it needs to go in the drain.
Right, salt will help for now, and if you can safely chip a little of the snow off the grate, that can help the melt drain, but don't put yourself in the road to do it.
Is private lane, so no cars. I will ask the maintenance man. Okay. Thank you, bye-bye.
You're welcome. Have a good afternoon. Bye now.
